source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 19 (PDF 137-155, printed 133-151); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 19 (Nuclear and Particle Physics), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.

blocks.prompt: 1 The neutron was discovered in 1932 by:
blocks.explanation: Rutherford predicted a neutral particle in 1920; James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932 (introduction).

book_ref.quote: The prediction came true when James Chadwick discovered neutron in 1932.

blocks.prompt: 2 Rutherford's experiments of 1911 showed that the atom has:

options.text: a uniform spread of positive charge
a dense, positively charged central part of very small size
neutrons spread all over its volume

blocks.explanation: The 1911 experiments indicated a dense, positively charged nucleus of very small size surrounded by electrons (introduction).

book_ref.quote: Ernest Rutherford's experiments in 1911 indicated the existence of a dense, positively charged central part

blocks.prompt: 3 From the α-particle scattering experiments, Rutherford concluded that:

options.text: most of the atom is empty and its mass is concentrated in the nucleus
the mass of the atom is spread evenly
electrons carry most of the mass of the atom

blocks.explanation: Rutherford concluded that most of the atom is empty and the mass is concentrated in a very small region, the nucleus (Do you know? box).

book_ref.quote: most of the part of an atom is empty and that mass is concentrated in a very small region called nucleus

blocks.prompt: 4 In the nuclide symbol ᴬ_Z X, the mass number A gives the number of:
blocks.explanation: A is the mass number: the total number of nucleons, i.e. protons plus neutrons (introduction).

book_ref.quote: 'A' stands for mass number which indicates the total number of nucleons (protons and neutrons)

blocks.prompt: 5 The number of neutrons in the nucleus ¹³¹₅₃I is:
blocks.explanation: N = A − Z = 131 − 53 = 78 (introduction).

book_ref.quote: The number of neutrons 'N' in the nucleus is given by A-Z.

blocks.prompt: 6 In the symbol ²³⁹₉₄Pu, the number 94 is the:

options.text: atomic (charge) number, the number of protons

blocks.explanation: The lower number Z is the atomic or charge number and gives the number of protons (introduction).

book_ref.quote: 'Z' the atomic or charge number which indicates the numbers of protons

blocks.prompt: 7 Using the orders of magnitude in the chapter (nucleus 10⁻¹⁴ m, atom 10⁻¹⁰ m), the atomic radius is about how many times the nuclear radius?
blocks.explanation: 10⁻¹⁰ m / 10⁻¹⁴ m = 10⁴ (introduction).

book_ref.quote: The nucleus is very dense with a radius of the order 10⁻¹⁴ m

blocks.prompt: 8 Experiments show that the mass of a nucleus is:

options.text: always less than the total mass of its separate protons and neutrons
always greater than the total mass of its protons and neutrons
exactly equal to the total mass of its protons and neutrons
equal to the mass of its protons only

blocks.explanation: The mass of a nucleus is always less than the sum of the masses of its nucleons; the difference is the mass defect (19.1).

book_ref.quote: the mass of the nucleus is always less than the total mass of all the protons and neutrons making up the nucleus

blocks.prompt: 9 The missing mass when nucleons combine to form a nucleus is called:
blocks.explanation: The lost or missing mass is called mass defect, Δm = [Zmₚ + (A − Z)mₙ] − m_nucleus (Eq. 19.1).

book_ref.quote: The lost or missing mass is called mass defect

blocks.prompt: 10 The energy equivalent of the mass defect Δm is given by:
blocks.explanation: The missing mass is converted to energy by Einstein's relation ΔE = (Δm)c² (Eq. 19.2).

book_ref.quote: The missing mass is converted to energy, used in the formation of the nucleus.

blocks.prompt: 11 Binding energy of a nucleus is defined as the:

options.text: energy needed to remove one electron from the atom
kinetic energy of the nucleons inside the nucleus
work done on the nucleus to break it into its neutrons and protons
energy given out when a nucleus emits an α-particle

blocks.explanation: Binding energy is the work done on the nucleus to break it into its constituent neutrons and protons (19.1).

book_ref.quote: The work done on the nucleus to break it into constituents neutrons and protons.

blocks.prompt: 12 Binding energy per nucleon is the:

options.text: energy needed to remove one proton only
average energy needed to separate a nucleus into its individual nucleons, per nucleon
total energy of all the electrons

blocks.explanation: Binding energy per nucleon is the better measure: the average energy needed to separate the nucleus into its individual nucleons (19.1).

book_ref.quote: average energy needed to separate a nucleus into its individual nucleons

blocks.prompt: 13 Binding energy is taken as negative, like absolute gravitational potential, because that potential is taken as zero:

options.text: on the surface of the Earth
at the centre of the Earth

blocks.explanation: Absolute gravitational potential is zero at infinity, so bound energies are negative (book correction in 19.1).

book_ref.quote: Absolute gravitational potential is taken as zero at infinity

blocks.prompt: 14 One atomic mass unit (1 u) is defined as:

options.text: 1/12 of the mass of an atom of carbon-12
1/16 of the mass of an oxygen atom
the mass of one hydrogen atom

blocks.explanation: 1 u is one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom (book correction in 19.1).

book_ref.quote: 1 u is one-twelfth (1/12) of the mass of an atom of carbon-12

blocks.prompt: 15 In kilograms, 1 u is equal to:

book_ref.quote: We usually use the masses of sub-atomic particles in atomic mass unit

blocks.prompt: 16 The mass of a helium-3 nucleus (2 protons, 1 neutron) is 5.006412 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. With mₚ = 1.672623 × 10⁻²⁷ kg and mₙ = 1.674929 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, its mass defect is:

book_ref.quote: Find the mass defect and binding energy of the helium nucleus given that

blocks.prompt: 17 A nucleus has a mass defect of 1.3763 × 10⁻²⁹ kg. Taking c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ and 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, its binding energy is about:

book_ref.quote: This energy can be calculated from Einstien's mass-energy relation:

blocks.prompt: 18 A tritium nucleus (A = 3) has a binding energy of 8.51 MeV. Its binding energy per nucleon is about:
blocks.explanation: B.E per nucleon = 8.51 MeV / 3 = 2.84 MeV (19.1).

book_ref.quote: A better measure is the binding energy per nucleon.

blocks.prompt: 19 In the chapter's table of masses, the entry 1.007276 u is the mass of:
blocks.explanation: The book correction says 1.007276 u is the proton's mass; the hydrogen-1 atom is 1.007825 u (19.1).

book_ref.quote: In the table, 1.007276 u is the mass of the proton

blocks.prompt: 20 To break a nucleus apart into its protons and neutrons:
blocks.explanation: Energy must be supplied to break the nucleus into its constituent protons and neutrons (For Your Information, 19.1).

book_ref.quote: Energy must be supplied to break the nucleus apart into its constituent protons and neutrons

blocks.prompt: 21 The binding energy curve is a graph of binding energy per nucleon against:
blocks.explanation: The curve plots binding energy per nucleon against the nucleon number A (binding energy per nucleon).

book_ref.quote: It is useful to draw a graphical curve of binding energy per nucleon against the nucleon number

blocks.prompt: 22 The binding energy of the ordinary hydrogen nucleus (one proton) is:
blocks.explanation: A single proton has nothing to bind, so its binding energy is zero (Figure 19.1).

book_ref.quote: initially the hydrogen nucleus with just one proton has a binding energy zero

blocks.prompt: 23 The binding energy per nucleon reaches its maximum, about 8.7 MeV, for:
blocks.explanation: The curve peaks at about 8.7 MeV for iron-56 (⁵⁶₂₆Fe), the most stable nuclide.

book_ref.quote: The curve reaches a maximum value of about 8.7 MeV for that of iron

blocks.prompt: 24 According to the curve, the most stable nuclei have nucleon numbers between:
blocks.explanation: The region of most stable nuclei is between A = 50 and A = 80 (binding energy per nucleon).

book_ref.quote: The region of most stable nuclei is between nucleon number 'A' equal to 50 and 80.

blocks.prompt: 25 Binding energy per nucleon is less for:

options.text: very light and very heavy nuclei

blocks.explanation: Binding energy per nucleon is less for very light and very heavy nuclei; it is greatest in the middle (curve).

book_ref.quote: Thus binding energy per nucleon is less for very light and very heavy nuclei.

blocks.prompt: 26 Energy is obtained from a nuclear reaction when the binding energy per nucleon of the products:
blocks.explanation: Energy is obtained from any nuclear reaction in which the binding energy per nucleon of the products increases.

book_ref.quote: energy is obtained from any nuclear reaction in which the binding energy per nucleon of the products increases

blocks.prompt: 27 The large step on the curve from hydrogen to helium suggests that:

options.text: a large energy is released when hydrogen is converted to helium
helium cannot be formed from hydrogen
hydrogen is more stable than helium
energy must be supplied to form helium

blocks.explanation: The large fall from hydrogen to helium suggests a large energy release when hydrogen is converted to helium (curve).

book_ref.quote: The fall from hydrogen to helium is large

blocks.prompt: 28 Fusing a pair of light nuclei on the binding energy curve is not easy because it needs:

options.text: an extremely high temperature, as in the Sun and stars

blocks.explanation: Such a process is not easy to initiate and needs an extremely high temperature, as occurs naturally in the Sun and stars.

book_ref.quote: needs extremely high temperature such as occurring naturally in our Sun and other stars

blocks.prompt: 29 Nuclear fission of uranium by slow neutrons was discovered by:
blocks.explanation: Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann of Germany observed Ba, Kr and neutrons when slow neutrons hit uranium-235 (19.2).

book_ref.quote: Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann of Germany

blocks.prompt: 30 A reaction in which a heavy nucleus splits into two nuclei of roughly equal size with the release of energy is called:
blocks.explanation: This is the definition of a fission reaction (19.2).

book_ref.quote: A reaction in which a heavy nucleus like that of uranium splits up into two nuclei of roughly equal size

blocks.prompt: 31 Fission differs from other nuclear reactions in that:

options.text: the products are always heavier than uranium
the nucleus breaks into two nuclei of almost equal size and very large energy is released
only one neutron is produced and no nuclei

blocks.explanation: Fission gives two nuclei of almost equal size, and a very large amount of energy is given out (19.2).

book_ref.quote: two nuclei of almost equal size are obtained

blocks.prompt: 32 The energy released in the fission of one uranium-235 nucleus is about:
blocks.explanation: About 200 MeV is given out in the fission of one uranium nucleus (19.2).

book_ref.quote: in the fission of one uranium nucleus, about 200 MeV energy is given out

blocks.prompt: 33 In a balanced fission equation, which quantities are the same on both sides?

options.text: sum of the mass numbers and sum of the charge numbers

blocks.explanation: There is no difference between the sums of the mass numbers and of the charge numbers on the two sides (19.2).

book_ref.quote: there is no difference between the sum of the mass and the charge numbers on both sides of the equation

blocks.prompt: 34 In the fission ²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴⁴₅₆Ba + ᴬ_Z Kr + 3¹₀n, the krypton nucleus has:
blocks.explanation: Mass numbers: 235 + 1 = 144 + A + 3, so A = 89. Charge numbers: 92 = 56 + Z, so Z = 36 (19.2).

book_ref.quote: Two possible fission reactions of uranium are given below as an example:

blocks.prompt: 35 The binding energy per nucleon of uranium is about 7.6 MeV and that of its fission products barium and krypton is about 8.5 MeV. The energy given out per nucleon is about:
blocks.explanation: Energy per nucleon = 8.5 − 7.6 = 0.9 MeV (19.2).

book_ref.quote: the binding energy per nucleon for uranium is about 7.6 MeV

blocks.prompt: 36 Suppose a nucleus with A = 240 and binding energy per nucleon 7.5 MeV splits into fragments with 8.4 MeV per nucleon. The energy released is about:

book_ref.quote: This means that an energy 235 × 0.9 = 211.5 MeV is given out

blocks.prompt: 37 The fission of uranium-235:

options.text: can produce different pairs of fragments, such as Ba + Kr, Sn + Mo or Xe + Sr
always produces barium and krypton only

blocks.explanation: Fission does not always produce the same fragments; Eq. 19.3, 19.4 and 19.5 give Ba + Kr, Sn + Mo and Xe + Sr (19.2).

book_ref.quote: The fission process of uranium does not always produce the same fragments

blocks.prompt: 38 The fission fragments of uranium are:
blocks.explanation: All the fission products (fission fragments) are radioactive (19.2).

book_ref.quote: All of these products (fission fragments) are radioactive.

blocks.prompt: 39 Fission takes place very easily with slow neutrons in:
blocks.explanation: Fission takes place very easily with slow neutrons in uranium-235 and plutonium-239, which are mostly used (19.2).

book_ref.quote: fission takes place very easily with the slow neutrons in uranium-235 and plutonium-239

blocks.prompt: 40 Which statement about fission is correct?

options.text: it is possible in many heavy elements, not uranium alone
it happens only in light elements
it needs a temperature of 10 million °C

blocks.explanation: Fission is not confined to uranium alone; it is possible in many other heavy elements (19.2).

book_ref.quote: Fission reaction is not confined to uranium alone

blocks.prompt: 41 A fission reaction that continuously maintains itself by the neutrons it releases is called:
blocks.explanation: Using the emitted neutrons to cause more fissions so that the reaction maintains itself is a fission chain reaction.

book_ref.quote: This process is called fission chain reaction.

blocks.prompt: 42 When a uranium-235 nucleus absorbs a neutron and undergoes fission, the number of neutrons emitted is:
blocks.explanation: The nucleus breaks into two nuclei of almost equal masses and emits two or three neutrons (chain reaction).

book_ref.quote: breaks into two nuclei of almost equal masses besides emitting two or three neutrons

blocks.prompt: 43 In a thin sheet of fissile material, no chain reaction occurs because:

options.text: the neutrons escape into the air
the sheet absorbs all the energy

blocks.explanation: In a thin sheet the resulting neutrons scatter in the air and cannot produce a chain reaction (Fig. 19.4 a).

book_ref.quote: The resulting neutrons scatter in the air and so they cannot produce any fission chain reaction.

blocks.prompt: 44 The mass of uranium in which one neutron out of all those produced in one fission produces further fission is called:
blocks.explanation: This is the definition of critical mass (chain reaction box).

book_ref.quote: Such a mass of uranium in which one neutron, out of all the neutrons produced in one fission reaction, produces further fission is called critical mass.

blocks.prompt: 45 The volume of the critical mass of uranium is called:
blocks.explanation: The volume of the critical mass is called critical volume or size.

book_ref.quote: The volume of this mass of uranium is called critical volume or size.

blocks.prompt: 46 An atom bomb uses uranium whose mass is:

options.text: much greater than the critical mass

blocks.explanation: If the mass is much greater than critical, the chain reaction proceeds rapidly and a huge explosion results; the atom bomb works on this.

book_ref.quote: Atom bomb works at this principle.

blocks.prompt: 47 If the mass of uranium is less than the critical mass, the chain reaction:
blocks.explanation: Below critical mass the chain reaction does not proceed (chain reaction).

book_ref.quote: If the mass of uranium is less than the critical mass, the chain reaction does not proceed.

blocks.prompt: 48 An atomic reactor obtains steady energy because its uranium mass is kept:

options.text: much greater than the critical mass

blocks.explanation: At the critical mass the chain reaction proceeds at its initial speed, giving a source of energy; reactors work on this principle.

book_ref.quote: If the mass of uranium is equal to the critical mass, the chain reaction proceeds at its initial speed

blocks.prompt: 49 Cadmium is used in control rods because it:

options.text: absorbs a large number of neutrons without becoming unstable or radioactive

blocks.explanation: Cadmium can absorb many neutrons without becoming unstable or radioactive, cutting down the neutrons available for fission.

book_ref.quote: Cadmium is an element that is capable of absorbing a large number of neutrons without becoming unstable or radioactive.

blocks.prompt: 50 In a controlled chain reaction, the number of neutrons from each fission that, on the average, causes another fission is:
blocks.explanation: In a controlled chain reaction only one neutron, on the average, from each fission causes another fission, so energy is released at a steady rate.

book_ref.quote: only one neutron, out of all the neutrons created in one fission reaction, becomes the cause of further fission reaction

blocks.prompt: 51 An uncontrolled chain reaction in a large amount of uranium-235 produces:

options.text: a large amount of energy with a huge explosion in a very small time

blocks.explanation: When the neutrons cause more and more fissions, a large amount of energy with a huge explosion is produced in an extremely small time.

book_ref.quote: a large amount of energy along with huge explosion is produced

blocks.prompt: 52 In a nuclear power station, the reactor plays the same part as the:

options.text: furnace of a thermal power station

blocks.explanation: The reactor plays the same part as the furnace: there coal or oil burns, here fission produces heat (19.3).

book_ref.quote: the reactor plays the same part as does furnace in a thermal power station

blocks.prompt: 53 The energy released in fission first appears as:

options.text: kinetic energy of the fission fragments

blocks.explanation: The fission energy appears as kinetic energy of the fission fragments, which becomes heat by collisions (19.3).

book_ref.quote: This energy appears in the form of kinetic energy of the fission fragments.

blocks.prompt: 54 The most important part of a reactor, where the fuel is kept, is the:
blocks.explanation: The core is the most vital part; the fuel is kept there in cylindrical tubes (19.3).

book_ref.quote: The most important and vital part of a reactor is called core.

blocks.prompt: 55 In natural uranium, the share of uranium-235 is only about:
blocks.explanation: Natural uranium has only about 0.7% uranium-235; reactor fuel is enriched to 2.4-3.0% (19.3).

book_ref.quote: the quantity of ²³⁵₉₂U in the naturally occurring uranium is only 0.7 percent

blocks.prompt: 56 Besides enriched uranium-235, which are also used as reactor fuels nowadays?
blocks.explanation: Nowadays plutonium-239 and uranium-233 are also used as fuel (19.3).

book_ref.quote: Nowadays plutonium-239 and uranium-233 are also being used as fuel.

blocks.prompt: 57 The function of a moderator in a nuclear reactor is to:

options.text: cool the steam from the turbine
slow down the neutrons produced in fission

blocks.explanation: Moderators slow down the fast fission neutrons, since slow neutrons are more useful for fission (19.3).

book_ref.quote: The function of these moderators is to slow down the speed of the neutrons produced during the fission process

blocks.prompt: 58 Which of the following is used as a moderator?
blocks.explanation: Moderators are substances of small atomic weight such as water or heavy water (19.3).

book_ref.quote: The fuel rods are placed in a substance of small atomic weight, such as water or heavy water.

blocks.prompt: 59 Heavy water differs from ordinary water because its hydrogen is:

options.text: ²₁H, the heavy isotope of hydrogen

blocks.explanation: Heavy water is made of ²₁H, a heavy isotope of hydrogen, instead of ¹₁H (19.3).

book_ref.quote: Heavy water, it may be remembered, is made of

blocks.prompt: 60 Control rods made of cadmium or boron work because these elements:

options.text: absorb fast neutrons strongly and slow ones weakly
slow the neutrons without absorbing any

blocks.explanation: As the book correction says, cadmium and boron absorb slow (thermal) neutrons strongly; the neutrons reaching the rods have been slowed by the moderator.

book_ref.quote: Cadmium and boron absorb slow (thermal) neutrons strongly and fast neutrons only weakly

blocks.prompt: 61 In an emergency, a reactor is shut down by:

options.text: letting the control rods fall fully into the reactor

blocks.explanation: For an emergency or repair, control rods fall back into the reactor, stopping the chain reaction (19.3).

book_ref.quote: control rods are allowed to fall back into the reactor and thus stop the chain reaction

blocks.prompt: 62 The temperature of a reactor core rises to about:
blocks.explanation: Heat from the chain reaction raises the core temperature to about 500 °C (19.3).

book_ref.quote: The temperature of the core, therefore, rises to about 500 °C.

blocks.prompt: 63 In a nuclear power station, high temperature steam is produced from ordinary water in the:
blocks.explanation: Heat is carried from the core to the heat exchanger, where it produces high temperature steam from ordinary water (19.3).

book_ref.quote: In the heat exchanger, this heat is used to produce high temperature steam from ordinary water.

blocks.prompt: 64 The radiation symbol shown in the chapter is used to indicate:

options.text: an area where radioactivity is handled or artificial radiations are produced

blocks.explanation: The symbol is universally used to indicate an area where radioactivity is handled or artificial radiations are produced (Do you know?).

book_ref.quote: This symbol is universally used to indicate an area where radioactivity is being handled

blocks.prompt: 65 The total output capacity of Pakistan's nuclear power plants (Karachi and Chashma) is:
blocks.explanation: The total output capacity is more than 3000 MW (19.3).

book_ref.quote: with a total output capacity of more than 3000 MW

blocks.prompt: 66 The best place so far found to store nuclear waste is:

options.text: the bottom of old, very dry salt mines deep below the surface

blocks.explanation: Waste must not be dumped in oceans or reach drinking water; old dry salt mines thousands of metres deep are the best place found (19.3).

book_ref.quote: The best place so far found to store these wastes is in the bottom of old salt mines

blocks.prompt: 67 Radioactive wastes are classified into:

options.text: high level, medium level and low level

blocks.explanation: Radioactive wastes are of three types: high, medium and low level (Do you know?, 19.3).

book_ref.quote: Radioactive wastes are of three types i.e., high level, medium level and low level.

blocks.prompt: 68 Nuclear fuel loaded into a reactor can operate it for:
blocks.explanation: The fuel once loaded can operate the reactor for a few months; then the used fuel is replaced (19.3).

book_ref.quote: The nuclear fuel once loaded into the reactor can operate it for a few months.

blocks.prompt: 69 A nuclear reaction in which two light nuclei merge to form a heavier nucleus is called:
blocks.explanation: This is the definition of fusion reaction (19.4).

book_ref.quote: A nuclear reaction in which two light nuclei merge to form a heavy nucleus is called fusion reaction.

blocks.prompt: 70 Energy is given out when light nuclei fuse to form a nucleus with mass number less than about:
blocks.explanation: The binding energy per nucleon increases up to A = 50, so fusion giving a nucleus with A below 50 releases energy (19.4).

book_ref.quote: the binding energy per nucleon increases up to A = 50

blocks.prompt: 71 Compared with fission, a fusion reaction gives:
blocks.explanation: In a fusion reaction more energy per nucleon can be obtained than in fission (19.4).

book_ref.quote: In a fusion reaction, more energy per nucleon can be obtained as compared to the fission reaction.

blocks.prompt: 72 Fusion is difficult to produce mainly because:

options.text: the nuclei attract each other too strongly
work must be done against the electrostatic repulsion between the positive nuclei

blocks.explanation: The two positively charged nuclei must be brought very close; work has to be done against their electrostatic repulsion (19.4).

book_ref.quote: work has to be done against the electrostatic force of repulsion between the positively charged nuclei

blocks.prompt: 73 In the deuterium-deuterium fusion ²₁H + ²₁H → ³₁H + ¹₁H + 4.0 MeV, the energy per nucleon is:
blocks.explanation: Four nucleons take part: 4.0 MeV / 4 = 1.0 MeV per nucleon (Eq. 19.6).

book_ref.quote: In both of these reactions, about 1.0 MeV energy per nucleon is produced

blocks.prompt: 74 In the fusion ²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n + 17.6 MeV, the energy released per nucleon is about:
blocks.explanation: Five nucleons take part: 17.6 / 5 = 3.52 MeV per nucleon, far more than the 0.9 MeV per nucleon in fission (Eq. 19.8).

book_ref.quote: then 17.6 MeV energy is obtained

blocks.prompt: 75 The deuterium-tritium fusion releases 17.6 MeV. With 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J and c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, the mass lost is about:

book_ref.quote: During a fusion reaction some mass is lost and its equivalent energy is given out.

blocks.prompt: 76 The fusion fuels in the reaction that gives 17.6 MeV are:
blocks.explanation: The fuels are deuterium and tritium, ²₁H and ³₁H (book correction in 19.4); ¹₁H is a product of Eq. 19.6.

book_ref.quote: The fuels in these reactions are deuterium and tritium

blocks.prompt: 77 In research on fusion of ²₁H and ³₁H, the nuclei are given very large velocities using:
blocks.explanation: One method is to give the nuclei a very large velocity with an accelerator (Fig. 19.6); it cannot give energy continuously on a large scale.

book_ref.quote: give these nuclei a very large velocity with the help of an accelerator

blocks.prompt: 78 A fusion reaction started by an extremely high temperature is called:
blocks.explanation: At such extraordinarily high temperature the reaction is called a thermonuclear reaction (19.4).

book_ref.quote: the reaction that takes place is called thermonuclear reaction

blocks.prompt: 79 The temperature needed to start a fusion reaction is about:
blocks.explanation: The light nuclei reach the required speed at about 10 million degrees Celsius (19.4).

book_ref.quote: the temperature at which the required speed of the light nuclei can be obtained is about 10 million degrees Celsius

blocks.prompt: 80 In the testing of a hydrogen bomb, the fusion is triggered by:
blocks.explanation: The very high temperature can be had for a very short time in an atom bomb explosion; the hydrogen bomb is triggered by an atomic bomb (19.4).

book_ref.quote: during the explosion of an atom bomb this temperature can be had for a very short time

blocks.prompt: 81 Fusion is not yet used to produce electricity because:

options.text: it has not been brought under control like fission
it gives less energy than fission
its fuels are not available at all

blocks.explanation: Fusion has not yet been brought under control like fission, so it is not used to produce electricity (19.4).

book_ref.quote: this reaction has not been brought under control like a fission reaction

blocks.prompt: 82 Experimental fusion reactors called 'artificial Suns' heat hydrogen isotopes to over:
blocks.explanation: Reactors such as EAST and HL-2M/HL-3 heat hydrogen isotopes to over 100 million °C (For your information, 19.4).

book_ref.quote: They heat hydrogen isotopes to over 100 million °C

blocks.prompt: 83 Radioactive decay is random. This means that:

options.text: all atoms decay at the same moment
we cannot predict when a particular atom will decay
each atom decays after exactly one half-life
decay can be stopped by cooling

blocks.explanation: We cannot foretell when any particular atom will decay; it could decay at once or remain for thousands of years (19.5).

book_ref.quote: we cannot foretell about any particular atom as to when will it decay

blocks.prompt: 84 The fluctuations seen in decay curves are evidence that radioactive decay is:
blocks.explanation: Fluctuation in decay curves is evidence of the random nature of decay (19.5).

book_ref.quote: Fluctuation in decay curves is also an evidence of its random nature.

blocks.prompt: 85 The activity of a radioactive substance is:

options.text: the time for half the nuclei to decay
the total energy of its radiations
the number of nucleons in its nucleus
the number of particles it emits per second

blocks.explanation: Activity is the number of particles emitted per second (19.5).

book_ref.quote: The activity of a radioactive substance is the number of particles it emits per second.

blocks.prompt: 86 The SI unit of activity is:
blocks.explanation: The SI unit of activity is the becquerel: 1 Bq = 1 decay per second (19.5).

book_ref.quote: Its SI unit is Becquerel (Bq).

blocks.prompt: 87 The count rate recorded by a radiation detector is:
blocks.explanation: The count rate, the counts recorded per second, is directly proportional to the activity (19.5).

book_ref.quote: It has been found directly proportional to the activity.

blocks.prompt: 88 The time taken for the activity of a sample to decrease to half of any starting value is called:
blocks.explanation: This is the definition of half-life (19.5).

book_ref.quote: The time taken for the activity of a sample to decrease to half of any starting value is called half life.

blocks.prompt: 89 No radioactive element can decay completely because:

options.text: new nuclei are formed from the radiation
in each half-life only half of the remaining nuclei decay

blocks.explanation: In any half-life only half the nuclei decay, so an infinite time is needed for all atoms to decay (19.5).

book_ref.quote: an infinite time is required for all the atoms to decay

blocks.prompt: 90 The number of atoms decaying in a given period is proportional to:

options.text: the number of atoms present at the beginning of that period

blocks.explanation: The number decaying in a period is proportional to the number present at its beginning (19.5).

book_ref.quote: the number of atoms decaying in a particular period is proportional to the number of atoms present in the beginning of the period

blocks.prompt: 91 The decay constant λ of an element is equal to:

options.text: the fraction of atoms decaying per unit time
the time for half the atoms to decay

blocks.explanation: From ΔN = −λNΔt, λ is the fraction of the decaying atoms per unit time; its unit is s⁻¹ (19.5).

book_ref.quote: decay constant of any element is equal to the fraction of the decaying atoms per unit time

blocks.prompt: 92 The unit of the decay constant is:
blocks.explanation: The decay constant is a fraction per unit time, so its unit is s⁻¹ (19.5).

book_ref.quote: The unit of the decay constant is s⁻¹.

blocks.prompt: 93 The activity of a radioactive substance is:

options.text: the number of particles it emits per second
the total number of its nuclei

blocks.explanation: The activity of a radioactive substance is the number of particles it emits per second (19.5).

book_ref.quote: The activity of a radioactive substance is the number of particles it emits per second.

blocks.prompt: 94 A graph of the number of undecayed atoms against time is called:
blocks.explanation: The graph of number of atoms present against time is called the decay curve (Fig. 19.7).

book_ref.quote: This graph is called decay curve.

blocks.prompt: 95 A sample starts with N₀ radioactive nuclei. After 5 half-lives, the number left undecayed is:
blocks.explanation: After n half-lives, N = (1/2)ⁿN₀; (1/2)⁵ = 1/32 (19.5).

blocks.prompt: 96 Of N₀ radioactive nuclei, the number that have decayed after 3 half-lives is:
blocks.explanation: Decayed number = N₀(1 − 1/2ⁿ) = N₀(1 − 1/8) = 7N₀/8 (Eq. 19.11).

book_ref.quote: we can use the general formula for decayed radioactive nuclides

blocks.prompt: 97 A radioisotope has a half-life of 8 days. Of 4800 atoms present initially, how many decay in 24 days?
blocks.explanation: 24 days = 3 half-lives; atoms left = 4800 × (1/2)³ = 600; decayed = 4800 − 600 = 4200 (worked as Example 19.2).

book_ref.quote: The half-life of polonium

blocks.prompt: 98 The half-life of a radioactive element is related to its decay constant λ by:
blocks.explanation: Solving N = N₀e^(−λt) for N = N₀/2 gives T½ = 0.693/λ (Eq. 19.13).

book_ref.quote: When N reduces to N₀/2, t is known as half-life

blocks.explanation: A = λN = 2.0 × 10⁻⁹ × 4.0 × 10¹⁸ = 8.0 × 10⁹ Bq (Eq. 19.10, as corrected).

blocks.prompt: 101 According to the chapter, which of these has the shortest half-life?
blocks.explanation: U-238: 4.5 × 10⁹ years; Ra-226: 1620 years; radon: 3.8 days; U-239: 23.5 minutes, the shortest (19.5).

book_ref.quote: the half-life of radon gas is 3.8 days and that of uranium-239 is 23.5 minutes

blocks.prompt: 102 A stable element made radioactive by bombarding it with very high energy particles is called:
blocks.explanation: Bombardment excites the nuclei, which become unstable; such elements are called artificial radioactive elements (19.5).

book_ref.quote: Such radioactive elements are called artificial radioactive elements.

blocks.prompt: 104 A radioactive isotope can act as a tracer because inside a living organism it:

options.text: behaves very differently from the normal isotope
behaves just like the normal isotope, but its radiation shows where it is
is always absorbed by bones only

blocks.explanation: It behaves like the normal isotope, but its location and concentration are found easily by measuring the radiation it emits (19.6).

book_ref.quote: A radioactive isotope behaves in just the same way as the normal isotope inside a living organism.

blocks.prompt: 105 The tracer technique consists of:

options.text: destroying the stable atoms with neutrons
replacing stable atoms with radioactive atoms of the same kind and following them with a detector

blocks.explanation: Radioactive atoms are substituted for stable atoms of the same kind and the 'tagged' atoms are followed with a radiation detector (19.6).

book_ref.quote: to substitute radioactive atoms for stable atoms of the same kind

blocks.prompt: 106 In agriculture, mixing a small amount of radioisotope with fertilizer helps farmers to:

options.text: increase the half-life of the fertilizer
find the proper amount of fertilizer by measuring how much the plant takes up

blocks.explanation: A radiation detector measures how much fertilizer a plant takes up, so farmers learn the proper amount to use (19.6).

book_ref.quote: we can easily measure how much fertilizer is taken up by a plant

blocks.prompt: 107 Improved varieties of rice, chickpea, wheat and cotton have been developed through:
blocks.explanation: Radiation-induced mutations gave varieties with better structure, more resistance to disease and pests, and better yield (19.6).

book_ref.quote: improved varieties of certain crops such as rice, chickpea, wheat and cotton have been developed

blocks.prompt: 108 Radioisotopes of many elements are made easily by:

options.text: bombardment with neutrons and other particles
passing them through a magnetic field

blocks.explanation: Radioisotopes can be made easily by bombardment with neutrons and other particles; they are now inexpensive (19.6).

book_ref.quote: Radioisotopes of many elements can be made easily by bombardment with neutrons and other particles.

blocks.prompt: 109 Radioactive iodine is absorbed mostly by the:
blocks.explanation: Radio-iodine goes mostly to the thyroid gland, phosphorus to bones and cobalt to the liver (medical uses).

book_ref.quote: Radio-iodine, for example, is absorbed mostly by the thyroid gland, phosphorus by bones and cobalt by liver.

blocks.prompt: 110 A diseased or hyperactive thyroid gland absorbs radioactive iodine:

options.text: more than twice the amount of a normal gland
less than half of a normal gland
the same as a normal gland

blocks.explanation: A diseased or hyperactive gland absorbs more than twice the amount of a normal thyroid gland (medical uses).

book_ref.quote: A diseased or hyperactive gland absorbs more than twice the amount of normal thyroid gland.

blocks.prompt: 111 The circulation of blood can be studied using radioactive:
blocks.explanation: A similar method with radioactive sodium-24 is used to study blood circulation (medical uses).

book_ref.quote: study the circulation of blood using radioactive isotope sodium-24

blocks.prompt: 112 Ionizing radiation can be used against cancer because rapidly multiplying cells:

options.text: absorb more radiation and are destroyed more easily than normal cells

blocks.explanation: Experiments show rapidly multiplying cells absorb more radiation and are more easily destroyed than normal cells (medical uses).

book_ref.quote: those cells that multiply rapidly absorb more radiation and are more easily destroyed than normal cells

blocks.prompt: 113 Radioisotopes in capsules implanted in malignant tissue for local, short-range treatment are called:
blocks.explanation: Radioisotopes in capsules called 'seed' are implanted in malignant tissue for local, short-ranged treatment (medical uses).

book_ref.quote: radioisotopes in capsules known as 'seed' are implanted in the malignant tissue

options.text: the radiation also damages some healthy tissues

blocks.explanation: The radiation also damages some healthy tissues, so the dose must be carefully controlled (medical uses).

book_ref.quote: The patient undergoing radiation treatment often feel ill

blocks.prompt: 116 Annihilation takes place when:

options.text: a neutron is absorbed by cadmium
a particle and its antiparticle come close to each other

blocks.explanation: Annihilation happens whenever a particle and its antiparticle come close to each other (19.7A).

blocks.explanation: Two photons, each of 0.51 MeV, travel in opposite directions to conserve momentum (Example 19.4).

options.text: after being accelerated to nearly the speed of light
